label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Nana,

I'm writing this down instead of saying it out loud, because if I try on the phone I'll end up saying "anyway" and asking about the weather. So you get a letter. Denise is going to read it to you in the kitchen, and I'm sorry about that, but she's a better reader than I am.

First, I'm sorry I'm not there on the 21st. I looked at every swap I could think of, and nobody could take my on-call week, so I'm stuck in Toronto with my phone on the nightstand. Everyone keeps telling me it's fine. It's a little bit not fine. But I know you'd rather I stop feeling bad and go watch the game, so consider this me going to watch the game.

I want to say something plainly, because you'd hate it if I got fancy. You picked this. Nobody sat you down and made you. You looked at the house, the stairs, fifty-one years of everything, and you decided you were ready for a second floor with a big maple outside the window. I'm proud of you. Not in a "good for you, Nana" way. In a "that was honestly impressive" way. Most people wait until someone else makes the call. You made it.

Kathleen Street is going to feel strange without you in it, and I won't pretend otherwise. You raised half the family in that kitchen. All of us came and went through it, and the rest of us only showed up in the summers. For me, those summers were the best part of being a kid. I'd get dropped off with a bag and a sunburn, and within an hour I'd figured out the deal: if I dried the dishes, I could stay up and watch the Expos or the Jays on that little TV on the counter. Nobody else has ever negotiated with me like that, and I've been a pushover for a good deal ever since. Honestly, a lot of what I'm good at came from being the kid who dried dishes in your kitchen.

Then there's the crib. You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. I'd lose, you'd shuffle and say "again," and I'd lose again. The first time I finally skunked you, I was fifteen, and you didn't even blink. You went and made a whole pan of butter tarts and said, "Now you have to eat these with the loser." I think about that a lot. You didn't go easy on me so I'd feel good. You made me earn it, and then you rewarded me with butter tarts, which is the only fair system I've ever seen.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a card with a twenty-dollar bill taped inside. The note said, and I'm quoting, "for pizza, you look thin on the computer." I'm not going to say where the twenty went, but I'm pretty sure it went to pizza, which was the point.

Okay, the pager. Last Christmas my phone went off in the middle of dinner, and I stepped away for a sec. When I came back, you asked me, very seriously, whether the internet was broken again and whether I'd fixed it. Since then, every single time I call, the first question is "did anything break?" I can't tell if that's a joke at this point or just how you check on me. So here's your answer: nothing is broken right now. The internet's fine, and so am I. And if something does break, you'll be the first to know, because you always ask.

Now the part I can't joke my way through. I remember the back steps. Early mornings, you'd be out there with your tea before the sun was really up, and I'd come out in whatever I'd slept in and sit down next to you. You never said a word until your cup was finished. At first I thought that was just you being you. Eventually I figured out it was your way of saying the morning was yours and you'd share it when you were ready. Those mornings taught me how to sit quietly with someone, which sounds small, but I use it all the time. I'm going to miss that step. Not the concrete, obviously. The fact that the house had a place where that could happen.

I'm not writing this to make it a funeral. I think Grandpa Walt would have hated that too. I know it's been hard since 2019, and I know the house was full of him for a long time before it was just full of stuff. Moving to Elmwood doesn't erase any of that. You're taking the good parts with you, the way you always have. You just got smart enough to take them somewhere with less snow to shovel.

And Elmwood looks nice. I've seen the pictures. A room on the second floor, a big maple, a view of the parking lot, which I'm sure you'll have opinions about within a week. And they have a crib league. A crib league, Nana. Within a month you'll have taken money off half of them. Tell the church ladies to get ready, because I don't think they know what they're in for.

About the crib board. I asked Denise to make sure I got it, and I'm not going to pretend that isn't a bit of a power move. I want it, and I want to play on it. So here's the plan: I'm coming up the weekend of December 5th, as soon as rotation lets me. I'll walk into Elmwood, sit down across from you, and we'll play the first game in the new place. You deal. I'll try to win. You'll say "again," I'll lose again, and we'll both know exactly how it's supposed to go.

I love you. Thank you for the crib, the tarts, the twenty dollars, the Expos, the dishes, the tea, and for never once letting me win.

Love,
[your name]
